title: Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis
formal: For every real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), does there exist an integer \(q\ge3\) such that no q-SAT decider A has a bound \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{(1-\varepsilon)n(F)}(L(F)+1)^d\) for every valid q-CNF formula F, for any fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\)? The width q may depend on epsilon but is fixed independently of the input. Equivalently, is \(\lim_{q\to\infty}s_q=1\)? This is the deterministic Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis.
definitions: Fix an integer clause-width bound \(q\ge 3\). A q-CNF formula is a finite list of clauses, each a finite list of at most q literals. A literal is a variable \(x_i\) or its negation \(\neg x_i\), with \(1\le i\le n\). The variables that occur are exactly \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), so n counts distinct variables, not clauses or input bits. Repeated literals, repeated clauses and clauses containing both signs of a variable are allowed. A Boolean assignment satisfies the formula if every clause has at least one true literal. An empty clause is false; the empty conjunction is true and has n=0. For a completely specified binary encoding, let \(\operatorname{code}(a)\), for a nonnegative integer a, be \(1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary expansion of a+1, where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)\rfloor+1\). Encode n and the number m of clauses with this code, then each clause by its coded length followed by its literals. Each literal is a sign bit (0 for positive, 1 for negated) and the code of its variable index. All indicated lists must be fully present, with no trailing bits, valid indices and every declared variable occurring. Let L be the complete bit length. Ill-formed strings, including clauses wider than q, are rejected. No density, satisfiability-count, occurrence or input-distribution promise is imposed. A q-SAT decider A is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program and fixed finite tape alphabets, a read-only input tape and initially blank work tapes. Each transition reads or writes only the cells at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. The total transition count includes parsing, input access and all internal work. A must halt on all inputs, decide satisfiability exactly on valid q-CNF formulas, and reject malformed strings in polynomial time in their length. It receives no advice, random bits, quantum operations, oracle or precomputed instance information. The machine may depend on the fixed q. For a valid formula F, let \(t_A(F)\) be its runtime and \(n(F),L(F)\) its variable count and bit length. An exponent \(\alpha\ge 0\) is attainable at width q if there exist such a decider A and fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\) with \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{\alpha n(F)}(L(F)+1)^d\) for every valid q-CNF formula F. The constants are independent of F. Define \(s_q\) as the infimum of all attainable exponents. This set is nonempty because exhaustive assignment testing gives an attainable exponent 1, so \(0\le s_q\le1\). The infimum need not itself be attainable. Polynomial factors in L remain explicit, including when clauses are repeated many times. The chosen explicit syntax and malformed-input normalization do not impose a new satisfiability promise; they fix the bit model for the source’s exponential-rate question. The sequence \(s_q\) is nondecreasing: a decider for width q+1 also decides the width-q restriction after checking its syntax. Since every \(s_q\le1\), its limit exists. The quantified statement says that no fixed positive saving from the exponent 1 works for all fixed widths. Its negation is that there exists one real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) such that for each integer \(q\ge3\) there are a q-SAT decider \(A_q\) and constants \(C_q,d_q\) with \(t_{A_q}(F)\le C_q2^{(1-\varepsilon)n(F)}(L(F)+1)^{d_q}\) for every q-CNF formula F. The algorithm and polynomial factor may depend on q and the selected epsilon. There is no added requirement of one algorithm receiving q as an input, nor of an effective procedure generating \(A_q\) from q. Each individual machine is uniform over its formula inputs. Infima need not be attained; the equivalence uses the available slack between a limit below 1 and 1.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed deterministic all-width proposition, equivalently a proof that \(\lim_{q\to\infty}s_q=1\) or that this limit is strictly below 1. A refutation must establish one positive exponential saving valid at every fixed width, with the algorithm and polynomial factors allowed to depend on that width. A positive answer must exclude such a shared saving. Improvement at finitely many widths, a randomized algorithm, or a lower bound only under another unproved hypothesis does not by itself meet this criterion. The target is a yes/no assertion about the limit, not its numerical approximation.
why: SETH is one of the main assumptions used to explain why specific polynomial running-time exponents resist improvement. Settling it would test the foundation of a broad network of tight conditional bounds in strings, graphs, data structures, and exact exponential-time algorithms.

importance.reason: A principal organizing hypothesis of fine-grained complexity, connecting exact SAT complexity to tight running-time barriers across many algorithmic areas.

progress.text: Impagliazzo and Paturi study the optimal exponential rates of fixed-width satisfiability and their limiting rate, proving relations among widths under ETH. They do not prove the limiting rate equals one.
The textbook states deterministic SETH as Conjecture 14.2, distinguishes separate fixed-width algorithms from a single unrestricted CNF-SAT algorithm, and proves that SETH implies ETH.
Vassilevska Williams surveys fine-grained reductions from satisfiability hypotheses to polynomial-time problems, explicitly tracking the relevant models and forms of hypotheses.

Jiang and Cai report the randomized general-3-SAT bound \(O^*(1.307031578^n)\) and a separate stronger Unique-3-SAT bound. Their Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2 concern fixed width; these preprint claims do not settle the deterministic all-width hypothesis.

status_note: The precise deterministic statement remains an unproved hypothesis in the checked sources. The July 2026 preprint improves a fixed-width randomized analysis and does not supply the quantified deterministic refutation. Targeted later-work searches on 14 September 2026 found no verified resolution; its imported inequalities and numerical certificates were not independently verified.

context_blocks.text: Exhaustive search tries all \(2^{n}\) assignments and checks the formula each time. Restricting clause width supports much faster algorithms, particularly for small k. SETH accommodates these speedups: it says that no positive constant saving in the exponent survives uniformly across arbitrarily large fixed widths. It does not assert that 3-SAT needs essentially \(2^{n}\) time.

The order of quantifiers separates this statement from several nearby claims. A \(2^{0.9n}\)-time algorithm for every fixed k would refute SETH even if the polynomial factors and implementations depended on k. A family of bounds \(2^{(1- 1/k)n}\) would be compatible with it. A fast algorithm for unrestricted CNF-SAT would also refute it, but the failure of such an unrestricted algorithm is not the definition being used here.

ETH asks for a positive optimal exponential rate already at width three; SETH additionally asks that the rates approach one as width grows. Sparsification relates bounded-width formulas to bounded-density formulas and helps transfer these hypotheses through reductions. It does not make the two hypotheses equivalent. Proving either would go beyond \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\), which by itself allows intermediate running times such as \(2^{\sqrt{n}}\).

Fine-grained reductions turn this hypothesis into precise conditional barriers for familiar polynomial-time problems, including Orthogonal Vectors, edit distance, and graph-distance questions. The reduction must preserve the intended exponential saving, not merely be polynomial-time as in an NP-hardness reduction. When a reduction or resulting algorithm uses randomness, the corresponding randomized hypothesis must be tracked separately.

Jiang and Cai’s July 2026 preprint reports randomized bounds \(O^*(1.306969598^n)\) for Unique-3-SAT and \(O^*(1.307031578^n)\) for general 3-SAT, where \(O^*\) suppresses polynomial input factors. These are stated preprint results whose proof and numerical certification have not been independently verified here. In either case, fixed width three and internal randomness differ from a deterministic saving that holds at every fixed width.

The 2015 textbook explicitly cautions that its limiting-rate definition is more precise than the informal question about one unrestricted CNF-SAT algorithm. A negative answer may consist of separate algorithms for all fixed widths, sharing one positive saving in the exponential rate but not necessarily a uniform generator or a common polynomial input factor.

sentences: SETH asks whether the optimal deterministic exponential rates for fixed-width satisfiability approach one as the allowed width grows.
Every proposed constant saving from exhaustive search must fail at some fixed width.
To refute it, one saving must work at every fixed width, although the algorithms and polynomial factors may vary with that width.
Faster algorithms for width three, including recent randomized ones, do not meet that requirement.
The hypothesis underlies many precise conditional lower bounds, including problems whose algorithms already run in polynomial time.
